Seller of Nassim Park Residences four-bedder reaps $2.5 mil profit
article:
The most profitable condo resale over the week of Sept 29 to Oct 6 involved a four-bedder at Nassim Park Residences , a freehold condo in District 10.

The seller of the 3,477 sq ft unit on the third floor scored a profit of $2.5 million (18.5%) when it changed hands for $16 million ($4,602 psf) on Oct 2. It had been purchased for $13.5 million ($3,883 psf) in September 2015. The annualised gain is 1.5% over an 11-year holding period.

Despite the seven-figure profit, this is far from the most lucrative transaction at Nassim Park Residences. That record remains with a 2023 deal that netted $7.26 million in profit. It involved a 4,822 sq ft four-bedder that was resold for about $22 million, after the seller purchased it from the developer for $14.74 million in June 2008.

Completed in 2011, Nassim Park Residences is a low-rise development on Nassim Road. It has 100 units, with four-bedroom units and five-bedroom penthouses measuring between 3,175 and 8,008 sq ft.

Nassim Park Residences recorded two other resale transactions this year, going by caveats lodged. Both units were in the black, earning their sellers profits of $2.95 million and $4.15 million.

Next up on the list of most profitable deals was a four-bedroom unit at Hillington Green in the Hillview area.

On Oct 2, the seller of the 1,755 sq ft unit reaped a $2.02 million (233.7%) profit when it sold for $2.89 million. The price is more than three times its initial purchase cost of $866,970 in June 2004, translating to an annualised gain of 6% over a holding period of almost 21 years.

Based on caveats lodged, the transaction is Hillington Green’s most profitable deal thus far. It surpasses the previous record of $1.83 million set in July 2023, when another 1,755 sq ft unit fetched $2.85 million. The seller had bought it 21 years earlier for $1.02 million in May 2002.

Hillington Green is a 999-year leasehold condo on Hillview Avenue that was completed in 2002. It comprises seven residential blocks with 480 units — predominantly three-bedders sized between 1,335 and 2,465 sq ft.

URA data compiled by EdgeProp Singapore shows that Hillington Green logged 11 other resale deals this year, all of which were profitable. The units, which ranged from 980 to 2,465 sq ft, generated gains of between $293,800 and $1.8 million.

Meanwhile, the week’s steepest loss occurred at The Scotts Tower in District 9.

The resale of an 840 sq ft one-bedder resulted in a $1.36 million (42.7%) deficit when it fetched $1.82 million ($2,168 psf) on Oct 2.

It had been bought for close to $3.18 million ($3,783 psf) in April 2013, resulting in a 4% annualised loss over a 13.5-year period.

The deal ranks as The Scotts Tower’s sixth most unprofitable transaction. It is around $330,000 shy of the biggest loss of $1.69 million from the sale of an 872 sq ft two-bedder a year ago. The unit was sold for $1.83 million in September 2025, after it had been purchased from the developer for $3.52 million in 2013.

Completed in 2016, The Scotts Tower is a 231-unit, 31-storey condo located at the corner of Scotts Road and Cairnhill Road. It is a five-minute walk from Newton MRT interchange, which is a stop away from lifestyle and retail amenities along the Orchard Road shopping belt.

title: Freehold condo Amber Park in District 15 notches fresh record high of $3,170 psf
article:
Amber Park — a freehold condo in District 15 — ranked first among private non-landed residential developments setting new psf-price highs in the week of Sept 29 to Oct 6.

It posted a fresh record of $3,170 psf when a 1,109 sq ft three-bedder on the 19th floor fetched $3.52 million on Oct 6.

The sale edges out Amber Park’s previous price peak of $3,085 psf, set almost two years earlier from the sub-sale of a 463 sq ft one-bedder for $1.43 million in October 2023.

Located along Amber Gardens, Amber Park is a 592-unit condo launched for sale in 2019 and completed in 2023.

The new project replaces the previous condo, with the same name, that was originally built in the 1980s and was sold en bloc in 2017.

The current development has three residential blocks offering one- to five-bedroom units ranging from 463 to 2,336 sq ft, as well as four duplex penthouses measuring between 4,392 and 5,005 sq ft.

The highest quantum recorded at the new Amber Park was for a 4,392 sq ft duplex penthouse purchased from the developers for $13 million in August 2021.

Another District 15 project that registered a new psf-price record during the week was The Shore Residences .

The 103-year leasehold condo hit a high of $2,585 psf with the sale of a 1,141 sq ft, three-bedroom unit for $2.95 million on Oct 5.

The previous record at The Shore Residences was $2,330 psf, set in December 2024, when another 1,141 sq ft unit was transacted for $2.66 million.

Completed in 2009, The Shore Residences is a 408-unit condo on Amber Road in Marine Parade. It has one- to five-bedders ranging from 592 to 2,906 sq ft.

Marine Parade MRT Station is a 10-minute walk from the development, while Haig Girls’ School and Tanjong Katong Primary School are both within a 1km radius.

Resale activity at The Shore Residences has been brisk, with 16 deals recorded so far this year. Excluding the Oct 5 sale, the other 15 transactions were priced from $1,816 to $2,297 psf, involving units sized between 592 and 1,432 sq ft.

Over in District 9, Robertson Edge recorded the third-highest psf-price peak for the week.

The 999-year leasehold project set a fresh record of $2,218 psf when a 431 sq ft one-bedder sold for $955,000 on Oct 1.

That is the first time an apartment at Robertson Edge has crossed the $2,200 psf mark. It surpasses the previous record of $2,174 psf set in February 2013, which involved a 506 sq ft two-bedder that changed hands for $1.1 million.

Located along Tong Watt Road, Robertson Edge is a boutique development comprising just 70 apartments. Its one- to two-bedroom layouts span 398 to 1,173 sq ft.

The Oct 1 deal marks the second caveated transaction at Robertson Edge this year. On Sept 4, a 431 sq ft one-bedder fetched $909,000 ($2,111 psf).

No psf-price lows were recorded during the week.

title: Five-room flat at Boon Keng sets new town record of $1.64 mil
article:
A five-room flat at City View @ Boon Keng , a Design, Build and Sell Scheme (DBSS) development, has changed hands for $1.64 million ($1,302 psf) in October 2026. The sale set new price and psf records for five-room flats in Kallang/Whampoa.

The 1,259 sq ft flat at 9 Boon Keng Road is on the 34th to 36th storeys and transacted on Oct 15. Its 99-year lease commenced in 2011, leaving about 84 years remaining.

The sale surpassed the previous town record of $1,588,888 ($1,273 psf), set by a 1,248 sq ft five-room flat at 8A Upper Boon Keng Road in September 2026. That flat, part of Kallang Trivista , is on the 28th to 30th storeys.

Introduced in 2005, DBSS allowed private developers to design, build and sell public housing, giving buyers more choice in layouts and finishes. The flats remain subject to HDB ownership and resale rules. The government announced a halt to new DBSS land sales in 2011 following concerns over high launch prices. Just 13 developments were launched under the scheme, with the last, Pasir Ris One , launched in 2012.

Completed in 2011, City View @ Boon Keng comprises 714 flats across three 40-storey blocks. It occupies a city-fringe location near the junction of Boon Keng Road and Bendemeer Road.

Boon Keng MRT Station on the North East Line is a short walk away, while Bendemeer MRT Station on the Downtown Line is also within walking distance. Both lines serve the city centre.

Nearby amenities include Bendemeer Market and Food Centre and the shops along Bendemeer Road. City Square Mall and Aperia Mall offer further shopping and dining options, alongside the eateries along Jalan Besar and Serangoon Road . Schools in the vicinity include Hong Wen School and Bendemeer Primary School.

title: Designing landscapes for 'non-humans': How Ng Sze Oun brings a site's history to life
article:
For Ng Sze Oun, landscape design goes beyond nature-based solutions and aesthetics to also consider “non-humans”.

“Designing for ‘non-humans’ could translate to designing for plants or nature, but that’s a very direct interpretation,” says the director of landscape studio Compound Collaborative.

Instead, the firm takes a broader view, uncovering the histories and ecological origins of a site. Ng describes this approach as “gossips in the garden”, weaving these stories into the landscape through features that visitors can discover and experience.

“Our aesthetic is not based on trends or what people hope to see or expect, but on what the site needs and its origins,” he adds.

Preserving traces of the past

One of Compound Collaborative’s recently completed projects is the landscape design for Dabu Hakka Building.

The seven-storey development in Geylang was officially opened by the Char Yong (Dabu) Association on July 3.

Conceived as a cross-generational civic centre celebrating Singapore’s Hakka culture, the development provided an opportunity for Ng and his team to connect the site’s history and cultural heritage with the present.

Stone tiger sculptures anchor the development’s landscape, with the designs first sketched by hand before being translated into three-dimensional images using AI.

“We cannot inherit the whole past, but we can preserve fragments of its memory,” says Ng.

This approach was likewise applied to the artwork at Dabu Hakka Building, where mud collected from the site was mixed with plaster to create a painting that preserves a physical trace of the place.

At the 128-key Varel Singapore boutique hotel, which occupies the former site of Selegie Centre , Compound Collaborative took a similar approach, drawing on the site’s history to inform its landscape design.

“We joined at the final stages of the design planning,” recalls Ng.

The main check-in lobby and reception of the hotel, which is located at the junction of Mackenzie Road and Selegie Road, are on the second floor, while much of the building is situated on the third floor and above.

This elevated structure left the first floor open for the firm to introduce a dense tropical landscape reminiscent of Singapore’s original rainforest.

“We thought the ground level could return to nature, back to Selegie’s history, which used to be a swampy and forested area,” says Ng.

Beyond its visual appeal, he adds that the greenery also serves as a buffer against noise and pollution from the surrounding busy streets.

Greening Singapore’s built environment

In a land-scarce country like Singapore, Ng believes the future of landscape design lies in integrating more greenery into existing buildings and urban spaces, rather than expanding development into natural areas.

He emphasises the importance of biophilic design, which reflects humans’ innate desire to connect with nature.

“After a hectic day in the city, being surrounded by greenery, especially when it is freely accessible, makes you feel great,” says Ng.

At 18 Cross, a mixed-use commercial development formerly known as Cross Street Exchange in the CBD, Ng focused on designing for the coexistence of human activity and wildlife within the same urban space.

Working alongside Benoy Architects, Compound Collaborative introduced façade-mounted green walls, with native wildflower species planted across the upper third of each wall to attract pollinators such as butterflies and bees.

The lower section features plants chosen for their visual appeal, catering to people who enjoy photographing the greenery while allowing pollinators to thrive at a distance from human activity.

Ng says the aim is to give people access to nature without encroaching too heavily on natural habitats or disturbing the wildlife that lives in them.

Over the next 10 to 20 years, he hopes to see more constructed nature integrated into buildings, alongside pocket parks that bring greenery closer to where people live and work.

Designing in response to the site

Compound Collaborative has also taken on overseas projects, including Three Sixty North, an ultra-luxury residential development in the Indian city of Gurugram.

With Gurugram facing severe air pollution, Ng and his team first studied the factors contributing to the poor air quality before developing a landscape design that residents could enjoy despite the challenging conditions.

Crop-residue burning in neighbouring Punjab contributes to seasonal pollution. Winds carry smoke towards Delhi and Gurugram, where winter weather conditions can cause pollutants to linger.

At Three Sixty North, the firm incorporated several features to address the local environment, including pavilions fitted with west-facing screens to shield users from blowing sand.

The landscape design also includes deployable filtration fabric to capture airborne particles, as well as dense layers of planting that help filter dust and provide a greener environment for residents.

“For a project to really respond to the site, we need to do research on its context and histories,” says Ng.

title: Boutique serviced apartment APT. opens its doors at newly revamped Stamford Place
article:
Boutique serviced apartment APT. has made its debut at Stamford Place , offering flexible stays ranging from six nights to a few weeks.

It comprises 66 serviced apartments across seven room types. The APT. Studio, APT. Deluxe and APT. Urban, measuring between 258 and 409 sq ft, cater to shorter stays. Each apartment comes with a king-sized bed, dedicated workspace, minibar and under-bed luggage storage.

For longer stays, guests can choose from the Stamford Suite, Stamford Premier Suite, and Hill Suite, measuring between 377 and 409 sq ft. The largest room types are the 506 sq ft Canning Suites and Civic Suites, which feature a separate living area, kitchenette, as well as an in-room washer and dryer.

The serviced apartment occupies the third and fourth floors of Stamford Place, which underwent an 18-month restoration and repositioning.

The former Stamford Court was acquired by a joint venture between boutique real estate investment firm Elevate Capital Group and global asset manager PGIM for $132 million in August 2024.

“APT. was created in response to the increasingly fluid way modern travellers live, work and move through the world,” said Ashish Manchharam, founder and managing partner of Elevate Capital Group.

“Stamford Place forms a key part of our wider vision to give the landmark renewed purpose, creating a place where people can stay, work, dine and connect.”

Guests at APT. can enjoy amenities including a 24-hour gym, reception and concierge services, and laundry facilities.

The 24-hour gym at APT. (Photo: APT.)

They will also have access to The Great Room by Industrious, a 30,000 sq ft workspace offering hospitality-led coworking areas, private suites and meeting rooms.

The ground level of Stamford Place houses eight F&B and retail spaces, including Blue Label Tavern for stone-fired pizzas; Yoruya, a new Japanese dining concept; and Cold Storage On The Go, which offers grab-and-go options and everyday essentials.

Located at the intersection of Stamford Road and Hill Street in Singapore's Civic District, Stamford Place is within a four-minute walk of City Hall MRT Station.

Elaine Luei, residence manager of Stamford Place and APT., said: “With workspaces, dining and culture woven into Stamford Place and the wider Civic District, the experience is designed to help guests settle in quickly, live comfortably and feel connected to the city rather than simply stay in it.

title: Spike in number of new private homes sold in September 2026 as larger-quantum deals dominate
article:
Property developers in Singapore moved 296 new homes — excluding executive condos (ECs) — this September, up 16.1% y-o-y and surging 93.5% from August, according to data released by URA on Oct 15.

Sales spiked as the Lunar Seventh Month — also known as the Hungry Ghost Festival, when sales activity tends to be muted in the absence of major new launches — came to an end on Sept 10.

A large share of September’s transactions were also for higher-priced properties.

Of the 296 new private homes sold last month, 19 were landed properties — the highest monthly volume since April 2018, said Huttons Asia CEO Mark Yip.

Explore comprehensive data about all ECs , including the average profit at 5 and 10 years

“Significant wealth accumulation over the years has enabled more Singaporeans, many already staying in private residential property, to purchase new landed homes,” Yip noted.

At the same time, the price premium for a new terrace home over a resale unit narrowed to 20.8% in the third quarter of 2026, down from 27.7% in the second quarter. That prompted buyers to consider a new terrace home, in Yip’s view.

By region, the Rest of Central Region (RCR) or city fringe, and the Outside Central Region (OCR) or suburbs, together accounted for 256 units or 86.5% of total developer sales (excluding ECs) in September.

SRI head of research and data analytics, Mohan Sandrasegeran, said the RCR made up the biggest share at 44.3%, or 131 units sold, while the OCR accounted for 42.2% with 125 units sold.

The Core Central Region (CCR) or prime areas represented about 13.5% of 40 units.

More units launched for sale

The number of new homes put on the market in September was also higher at 158. That is up 36.2% m-o-m from 116, and 7.9 times the year-ago volume of just 20 units launched in September 2025, according to Huttons.

Amberwood at Holland was the only condo project launched last month, with 24 units sold.

More than 60% of these units transacted were four-bedroom and five-bedroom apartments, given Amberwood’s appeal to families. Two-thirds of the homes sold at the condo were also priced above $3 million, which Yip reckons may have limited the demand pool.

The CCR project debuted on Sept 25, moving 11% of its total 212 units at an average price of about $3,019 psf . If going by the 70 units released in the first phase, the take-up rate was 33% at launch.

Demand for Amberwood at Holland was primarily driven by owner-occupiers and families drawn to the spacious homes and low-density living concept, said Chistine Sun, chief researcher and strategist of Realion (OrangeTee & ETC) Group.

The best-selling project by volume was Terra Hill with 32 units sold at a median price of $2,209 psf, followed by The Sen with 25 units transacted at a median of $2,386 psf.

ERA CEO Marcus Chu said: “Attractive pricing may have been a key factor in the rebound in sales… The median new-sale prices for both [Terra Hill and The Sen] were below the wider RCR equivalent of $2,522 psf for new non-landed private homes in September.”

Amberwood at Holland took third place. Lentor Gardens Residences and Dunearn House also made the list of best-selling projects. Sandrasegeran noted that the continued sales at such projects, after their launches in July, “suggest that buyer interest has extended beyond their initial launch periods”.

“This is particularly noteworthy given the relatively quieter primary market environment in August and September,” he added.

Meanwhile, among landed residential projects, Luxus Hills moved 18 terrace houses and Belgravia Ace sold nine semi-detached, strata landed units in September.

The landed home sales pushed up the median quantum of units sold in the OCR to $3.2 million for the month, Huttons' Yip said.

And in the first nine months of this year, developers launched an estimated 4,790 units for sale, which is down 41.9% y-o-y as compared to the 8,247 units in the same period last year.

Sales totalled around 5,334 units in the first nine months, falling by 30.4% y-o-y.

Sandrasegeran said the lower transaction volume for the nine-month period should be viewed in the context of a relatively limited new-launch pipeline during the year, with several government land sales (GLS) sites awarded in earlier periods expected to enter the market only in 2027.

Homes that fetched $2.5 million and above

Given the larger-quantum deals that were sealed at Amberwood at Holland, Belgravia Ace and Luxus Hills in September, almost 65% of the transactions in the month were within the price range of $2.5 million to below $10 million, Huttons data showed.

Chu from ERA likewise pointed out that strong take-up of three- and four-bedroom homes at existing projects such as Lentor Mansion and Terra Hill drove much of the volume in the $2.5 million to $3 million price range.

The priciest deal involved a 2,088 sq ft unit at Skywaters Residences , sold to a Singaporean for $11.48 million.

It is also the only ultra-luxury condo unit sold for at least $10 million in September, compared to none in August, according to Realion’s Sun.

This was followed by the sale of two semi-detached homes on Upper Neram Road and Aida Street, for $8.9 million and $8.6 million, respectively.

Sun noted that luxury home demand remained firm, with two new non-landed homes in the CCR sold for at least $5 million but below $10 million. That is up from one transaction in the previous month.

Both of those units were 2,056 sq ft apartments at UpperHouse at Orchard Boulevard , fetching $7.8 million and $7.3 million.

New EC sales remain soft

In the EC segment, developers sold 23 new homes in September, up 27.8% m-o-m from the low base of 18 units sold in August.

Coastal Cabana continued to lead new EC transactions for the fourth straight months, with 19 units moved at a median of $1,811 psf, according to ERA.

Rivelle Tampines , which launched in March, accounted for two of the remaining new EC units sold. Altura and Otto Place each logged one transaction.

“Fresh supply has been limited in the EC market with no new EC project rolled out since Rivelle Tampines,” said PropNex. “URA figures showed that just 145 EC are unsold in launched EC projects at the end of September.”

More active launch pipeline expected to support 4Q2026 sales

Looking ahead, new home sales momentum is likely to continue into October, as a more active fourth-quarter launch pipeline kicks off.

Lucerne Grand , situated on Lakeside Drive in Jurong, has already provided “an encouraging start to the quarter”, selling more than 61% of its units over its launch weekend on Oct 3–4, said Sandrasegeran.

At least three other private residential projects are set to book sales in the year’s final quarter.

The Serra Residences, launching on Oct 16, is one of two major freehold projects in the CCR coming on the market this year. It is located on Bassein Road in prime District 11.

Yip noted that freehold projects are scarce in Singapore, as they are dependent on housing developers redeveloping their freehold land bank or successfully acquiring a freehold site en bloc.

Meanwhile, Thomson Reserve is a highly anticipated mega project in the Thomson area, priced from $2,608 psf or $1.544 million. The 1,268-unit mega development is scheduled to debut on Oct 31, and will be the largest new private residential project to launch in Singapore this year.

Over on Stevens Road, The Park Residence is a 43-unit ultra-luxury freehold project that will feature large-format units of more than 4,000 sq ft each.

“We expect buyers to remain selective and will gravitate towards projects where location, layout and pricing line up,” PropNex wrote.

title: IOI Properties eyes Chijmes, Capitol Kempinski acquisitions in Singapore
article:
IOI Properties Group Bhd is in exclusive talks to acquire Singapore’s Chijmes and the nearby Capitol Kempinski hotel, while planning a private property fund initially comprising office assets valued at about S$6 billion, Bloomberg reported.

Group CEO Lee Yeow Seng told Bloomberg that due diligence on the potential acquisitions was underway, but declined to disclose the purchase consideration, citing ongoing negotiations.

The Capitol Kempinski hotel had been marketed for about S$600 million (about RM1.9 billion), Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Chijmes, a heritage retail and dining complex housed in a former Catholic convent in Singapore's civic district, was valued at S$379 million at end-2025.

Neither figure represents an agreed purchase consideration for the potential acquisitions.

According to Bloomberg, Singapore-based developer Perennial Holdings controls approximately one-third of Chijmes and 80% of Capitol Singapore, the broader development comprising the hotel, a retail mall and residential units.

Other investors include a vehicle backed by an unnamed Southeast Asian sovereign wealth fund. Perennial did not respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.

Lee said IOI Properties was in discussions to introduce high-end fashion retailers at Chijmes to improve its tenant mix and rental income, which he said had been constrained by the complex's concentration of food and beverage outlets.

The group also wants to introduce an international ultra-luxury hotel brand to replace Kempinski if the hotel acquisition proceeds, according to Lee.

Private fund to support expansion

The potential acquisitions come as IOI Properties seeks to establish a private real estate investment fund to bring outside investors into its Singapore commercial property portfolio.

Lee told Bloomberg that the proposed fund was expected to be established within two months and would initially comprise two office assets with a combined value of approximately S$6 billion.

These are the office component of South Beach and IOI Central Boulevard Towers, the group's landmark office development in Singapore's central business district.

Former Pimco Prime Real Estate executive Varun Singh has been tapped to oversee the proposed fund.

Lee said the group had approached prospective investors, including private equity firms, sovereign wealth funds and insurance companies, but declined to identify them.

The fund is targeting an internal rate of return of 10% to 11%, with distributions every six months.

Under the proposed structure, IOI Properties intends to reduce its ownership interests in the initial assets to approximately 50%, offering minimum investment holdings of about S$500 million with a five- to seven-year lock-up period.

The group also intends to inject additional Singapore properties into the fund over time, with a longer-term objective of listing the vehicle as a real estate investment trust (REIT).

Gearing in focus amid Singapore expansion

IOI Properties' expansion in Singapore has increased its borrowings, with net debt equivalent to approximately 85% of equity as at end-June, according to Bloomberg .

Lee said he aimed to reduce the ratio to between 30% and 50% over the next three to five years.

The group's Singapore acquisitions include buying City Developments Ltd's stake in South Beach to gain full ownership of the development, and purchasing the Asia Square Tower 2 office building.

The group is also pursuing other potential acquisitions in the city-state.

IOI Properties has jointly submitted an expression of interest with an investment entity managed by CapitaLand Investment Ltd to acquire a 100% interest in One Raffles Place on a proposed 50:50 basis, according to an Oct 12 report on the group's Bursa Malaysia filing.

The prospective buyers are undertaking due diligence and exclusive negotiations with the vendors. OUE REIT, the majority owner of the office complex, said on Oct 8 that no binding sale agreement had been executed.

Separately, IOI Properties announced on Oct 1 a conditional agreement to acquire Shenton 101 Pte Ltd, the owner of Shenton House , from Lee, its group chief executive officer and major shareholder, for a nominal consideration of S$1.

Under the proposed transaction, the group would also settle S$217.06 million in shareholder advances and consolidate Shenton 101's borrowings of S$376.23 million into its accounts upon completion. Both amounts were stated as at July 31, 2026.

title: Four-bedder at Bishan Park Condominium resold at $1.77 mil profit, the highest at the development
article:
A 1,550 sq ft, four-bedroom unit at Bishan Park Condominium changed hands for $2.28 million ($1,471 psf) earlier this month, according to URA caveats. The seller had bought it for $515,000 ($332 psf) in October 2006.

This translates to a profit of $1.77 million, or an annualised gain of 7.7% over nearly 20 years, excluding transaction and financing costs.

No resale at the development has been more profitable. The previous record gain of $1.55 million was made in January 2024 from the sale of a 1,507 sq ft four-bedroom unit (see Table 1).

Bought for $505,000 ($335 psf) in April 2004, the unit was sold for $2.05 million ($1,360 psf). This translates to an annualised gain of 7.3% over nearly 20 years.

The subject unit’s two previous owners on record both sold at a loss. The earlier owner bought it for $935,000 ($603 psf) in May 1997, shortly before the Asian Financial Crisis. In September 2001, that owner sold it for $640,800 ($413 psf), losing $294,200. The next owner sold it for $515,000 in October 2006, losing another $125,800.

Units at the development continue to change hands regularly, with 19 resale transactions in 2024 and 13 in 2025. Seven resale deals have been recorded at the development so far this year.

Based on caveats lodged, every resale at the development since 2011 has been profitable. All 43 recorded losses were incurred by owners who bought between 1995 and 2003.

Bishan Park Condominium is located along Sin Ming Walk in District 20, within the Rest of Central Region (see Map 1). Completed in 1994, the development comprises 320 three- and four-bedroom units across five blocks. It has a remaining lease of about 63 years.

Primary schools within a 1km radius include Ai Tong School, CHIJ St. Nicholas Girls’ School and Ang Mo Kio Primary School. For green space, parks close by include the Lower Peirce Reservoir Park and Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park.

The condominium is a short walk from Bright Hill MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line, which is set to become an interchange with the Cross Island Line by 2030.

Ultimately, the record gain suggests that demand for homes in the Bishan and Upper Thomson area remains firm, even for older leasehold developments.

Nearby, the new 1,268-unit Thomson Reserve condominium project is slated for launch on October 31 . CapitaLand Development and UOL Group are jointly developing the 99-year leasehold project, which is a two-minute walk to Upper Thomson MRT Station.

title: Hotel-to-hostel conversions in Hong Kong mark the birth of a genuine asset class
article:
From 2020 until recently, Hong Kong was a hard sell. Its borders stayed largely shut through the pandemic, and travel with mainland China did not fully resume until Feb 6, 2023.

Interest rates climbed, and the city’s property market went through a six-year correction that began in late 2019, driving down the values of offices, retail properties and warehouses. Today, capital is returning to Hong Kong, and one of the clearest signals is coming from an unlikely sector: student accommodation.

Hong Kong has set out to become Asia’s education hub, but its universities now admit more students from overseas and mainland China than they can house. To fill the gap, investors are buying hotels built for tourists and turning them into student hostels. Singapore’s CapitaLand Investment is among those pursuing the opportunity, with a proposed HK$2.3 billion ($380 million) deal for one such hotel.

Our view is simple: Student housing in Hong Kong has the makings of a lasting asset class, not just a passing trade. But what is driving the rush of capital, what returns can investors realistically expect, and where should they exercise caution?

Why investors stayed away

Before I get to why student beds are suddenly in demand, it helps to rewind a little. Why did so many investors walk away from Hong Kong in the first place?

Office values fell by about half from their 2018 peaks, while retail values declined by around 42%. Financing also became harder to secure. A CBRE survey ranked Hong Kong as the toughest major market in the region for raising property debt, while lending across Asia Pacific, excluding Japan, fell to a 16-year low in the first half of 2026. For many investors, sitting on the sidelines was the easier choice.

Hotels had problems of their own. Tourists returned, with 49.9 million arrivals in 2025. But they spent less than they used to. Overnight visitors spent HK$5,503 each in 2025, down from HK$6,614 in 2018. Day-trippers spent roughly half what they did before, while hotel room rates also came under pressure.

According to CBRE, average hotel room rates fell 11% y-o-y in early 2025.

For hotel owners, the search for a more reliable source of income was becoming increasingly urgent. As it turned out, another sector was facing a very different problem: demand was growing faster than supply.

Study, stay, work

Hong Kong wants to attract young talent and keep it. In September 2025, the Hong Kong government announced that the non-local student quota at publicly funded universities would rise from 40% to 50% from the 2026/2027 academic year.

The pitch is simple: Come to Hong Kong to study, then stay on to work. We regard this as one of the more coherent approaches to talent recruitment and retention in the region. It also gives the student accommodation sector a source of demand that does not depend on a recovery in the office market.

Hong Kong’s universities provide another draw. In the QS World University Rankings 2027, published in June 2026, the University of Hong Kong was placed 11th and the Chinese University of Hong Kong 18th. It was the first time two Hong Kong universities had ranked among the world’s top 20.

This year, Hong Kong overtook the US as the second most popular overseas study destination for students from mainland China. Hong Kong approved more than 94,500 student visas last year, more than double the number in 2022, according to an August 2026 article by Propmodo.

The challenge is finding accommodation for these students, as the supply of beds has failed to keep pace with demand.

Hong Kong had about 192,000 university students in the 2024/2025 academic year, but only around 44,000 hostel beds. That works out to more than four students for every bed, although not all students require hostel accommodation, and estimates of the actual shortfall vary. Savills puts the gap at around 88,000 beds, while JLL estimates a shortage of 76,300 beds in 2026, widening to 147,200 by the 2029/2030 academic year.

Regardless of the methodology, the shortfall is substantial. Private purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) has barely made a dent in the shortage, with only about 6,900 beds currently available and another 16,300 in the pipeline.

Rents tell a similar story. According to JLL, stabilised rents range from HK$7,000 to HK$10,000 per bed per month, or approximately $1,150 to $1,650. Student accommodation rents in Hong Kong have risen by 10% annually since 2022, while major developments are reporting occupancy rates of 98% to 100%.

Such strong demand has not gone unnoticed by investors.

When hotels become hostels

In July 2025, the Hong Kong government introduced the Hostels in the City Scheme, making it easier to convert hotels and other commercial properties into student accommodation.

To us, this is what good policy design looks like: removing regulatory obstacles rather than simply handing out subsidies. If demand is the fuel, the scheme provides the spark.

Under the Hostels in the City Scheme, a hotel converted into student accommodation remains classified as non-domestic. Owners can therefore avoid the lengthy rezoning and floor-area cuts that a switch to residential use would normally bring. In most cases, there is also no change to the land lease and no extra land premium to pay, potentially avoiding one of the biggest costs in a Hong Kong redevelopment.

The owners moved fast. By February 2026, the scheme had 25 applications covering about 5,100 beds. By September, 41 applications covering around 10,800 beds had been deemed eligible, reflecting the pace of investor interest.

Hotels led the way because they could be converted relatively quickly. They were already configured as rows of small rooms, and conversions typically take two to six months, compared with six to 18 months for offices. Faster conversion means rental income can begin flowing sooner.

What strikes us most is not the pace but the breadth of the buyer pool. In March, China Resources Longdation, part of a mainland state-owned group, paid HK$953 million for Hotel COZi Oasis in Kwai Chung, which will hold about 900 beds.

That same month, Centaline, best known as one of the city’s biggest property agencies, bought the 494-room Regal Oriental for HK$1.52 billion. Banks subsequently competed for a HK$1 billion financing mandate for its conversion.

Local developer Wang On teamed up with US private equity firm Angelo Gordon on Sunny House, a 720-unit conversion that is currently 98% occupied. In September, Singapore’s CapitaLand Investment moved to buy the 550-room ibis Hong Kong Central & Sheung Wan for HK$2.3 billion, one of the largest bets on the sector yet.

For such a young sector, the breadth of capital flowing in is striking. Mainland Chinese state-owned groups, local property agencies and banks, US private equity firms, and now one of Singapore’s largest real estate managers are pursuing opportunities in the same market.

But with so much money chasing these assets, the obvious question is: What kind of returns can investors actually expect?

What investors can expect

The answer depends very much on the asset. Industry estimates provide a useful benchmark, but they are no guarantee of actual returns.

JLL’s research estimates that office-to-student accommodation conversions could achieve target internal rates of return of 15% to 18% over a five-year holding period, compared with 13% to 16% for hotel conversions. These are target returns, however, and actual performance will depend on rental income, occupancy rates, operating costs and the eventual sale price.

Much of the appeal lies in the nature of the income. Nick Tang, CEO and executive director of Wang On, describes student housing as offering “stable and predictable income”.

Lenders appear to recognise that appeal, too. Bank of China (Hong Kong), for instance, reportedly competed against Industrial Bank’s Hong Kong branch and other lenders for the HK$1 billion loan mandate for the Regal Oriental conversion.

When banks compete to lend in a market where property financing is otherwise difficult to secure, it tells us they see something attractive in the underlying income. I think that is significant. But the competition for selected deals should not be mistaken for a broader recovery in property lending.

The UK offers a glimpse of what a mature student housing market looks like. Investors poured GBP2.1 billion ($3.56 billion) into UK PBSA in the first quarter of 2026 alone. Knight Frank puts prime London net initial yields at around 4.5%, compared with 5.25% to 5.5% in regional markets.

Hong Kong is still some way from that level of market maturity. That early stage is part of the appeal. It is also where much of the risk lies.

The risk of arriving late

Every property boom eventually reaches a point where early investors have made their money and latecomers risk paying too much. Hong Kong’s student housing market may not be there yet, but the warning signs are worth watching.

The first is price. Colliers senior director of hotel advisory Shaman Chellaram has cautioned that the remaining opportunity is “diminishing quite quickly” as more capital pours into the sector. More bidders mean higher acquisition prices, and higher entry costs mean thinner returns.

Then there is the question of how much demand each property can realistically capture. The citywide shortage is real, but so is the rush to fill it.

A shortage across Hong Kong does not mean every building will benefit equally. Students generally prefer to live near campus, and accommodation an hour away is a harder sell.

The pipeline of 16,300 beds is more than double the existing purpose-built supply. Even developers acknowledge “a real probability of oversupply in the next few years”. Oversupply in the wrong locations and scarcity in the right ones can easily co-exist.

Then there is policy risk. Much of the increase in demand has been driven by Hong Kong’s decision to admit more non-local students, alongside mainland Chinese families increasingly viewing the city as an alternative to the US.

But policies change, and so do family choices. If either shifts, the flow of incoming students could slow.

I do not expect demand to reverse, but I would be cautious about assuming today’s rental growth and occupancy rates will continue indefinitely. In a more crowded market, realised returns could drift towards the lower end of expectations, with a widening gap between winners and losers.

This is an operating business

If there is one point I want investors to take away, it is this: Owning student housing is closer to running a business than simply collecting rent.

Rooms turn over every academic year, so occupancy must be rebuilt annually.

Student welfare, community, safety and university relationships all influence whether beds are filled at the projected rents. In mature markets, the difference between strong and weak operators is reflected directly in net operating income.

In Hong Kong, where the sector is still young and operating track records are limited, I believe choosing the right operator may be just as important as choosing the right building, if not more so.

Prudent investors should therefore test whether their investments remain viable if rental growth slows, occupancy falls or operating costs rise. Stability is the product of good operations. It does not come with the title deed.

The Hostels in the City Scheme also comes with restrictions. Converted properties must reserve at least 90% of their places for eligible students, limiting operators’ flexibility to accommodate other tenants if student demand weakens.

That restriction does not undermine the investment case, but it is another reminder that these assets cannot simply be treated as conventional rental properties.

The real test is the exit

The exit matters as much as the entry. Yet while much of the market is focused on getting in, I am more interested in the exit.

According to Real Estate Asia, buyers today are predominantly family offices, private investors, private equity funds and state-owned enterprises. Pension funds, insurers and sovereign wealth funds are expected to follow, but only once assets have matured and established a track record.

That institutional participation could ultimately broaden the buyer pool, improve liquidity and help establish long-term pricing for the asset class.

Hong Kong is still at the beginning of that journey. If it follows even part of the UK’s path, early investors holding well-located, professionally managed and stabilised assets could benefit as institutional capital enters the market and yields compress.

If that institutional demand fails to materialise, however, investors could find themselves holding an operating business with a limited pool of potential buyers, in a market where refinancing remains difficult.

For anyone buying today, the eventual sale may depend on whether larger institutional investors are willing to pay for the income stream that has been built.

That is why asset selection matters so much. Institutions typically seek assets with proven operating histories, and building that track record takes years of sustained occupancy and reliable income.

The properties that institutional investors may eventually want to own are being selected, developed and operated today. Not every hostel will make the cut.

What Singapore investors should take from this

For Singapore investors, student housing offers a way to participate in Hong Kong’s recovery without betting on a rebound in offices or retail.

Hong Kong’s hotels were built for a city of tourists. Many are now being repurposed for a growing population of students. That shift says something about the city’s ability to adapt its existing real estate to changing demand.

The timing is worth noting. CapitaLand’s move shows that major Singapore investors are no longer merely watching this emerging sector from the sidelines.

Hong Kong is close and familiar, and its property market has been through years of repricing. Student housing offers exposure to a different source of demand, supported by the city’s education policies, internationally ranked universities and shortage of accommodation.

With more capital chasing opportunities in the sector, investors will need to be increasingly selective. Location matters, particularly proximity to universities and transport links. So does the track record of the operator, and whether the acquisition price still makes financial sense if rental growth slows or stalls.

I believe student housing has the makings of a lasting asset class, not a passing investment trend. But not every conversion will succeed, nor will every investor achieve the returns being projected. Those who do best will need conviction and discipline in equal measure.

For much of the past five years, the question was whether Hong Kong was worth the risk at all.

Today, the question is narrower and more useful: Which beds, where, and at what price?

Investors who answer that carefully may find that one of Hong Kong’s newest asset classes becomes one of its most enduring investment opportunities.

title: Thomson Reserve: First mega launch in eight years at Upper Thomson, priced from $2,608 psf
article:
The 1,268-unit Thomson Reserve will be the largest new private residential project to launch in Singapore this year, and the first mega development with more than 1,000 units to debut in 2026.

Occupying a sprawling 5ha site — equivalent to about seven football fields — the development has a prominent 500m frontage along Upper Thomson Road.

A VIP preview will be held on Friday, Oct 16, ahead of the public preview the following day. The official launch is scheduled for Oct 31.

It will be the first major new residential launch in the Upper Thomson–Shunfu neighbourhood in eight years, following the 1,206-unit JadeScape in 2018.

The 99-year leasehold Thomson Reserve is a redevelopment of the former Thomson View Condominium , which was sold en bloc for $810 million in November 2024.

The buyer was a consortium comprising CapitaLand Development (CLD), with a 50% stake, UOL Group (40%) and its subsidiary, Singapore Land Group (10%).

The acquisition marked the end of a 17-year collective-sale journey for Thomson View’s owners, who had made five attempts since 2007 before finally securing a buyer.

The $810 million purchase price translated into a land rate of $1,178 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr), after factoring in the land betterment charges and the lease top-up premium to a fresh 99 years.

"A large five-hectare site like Thomson Reserve gives us the opportunity to create a spacious development that merges architecture with nature, offering a differentiated product that captures an increasingly sought-after lifestyle that owners are looking for," says UOL Group CEO Liam Wee Sin.

"Such distinctive locational and design attributes, together with the limited supply, have generated keen interest in Thomson Reserve," adds Liam.

Proximity to nature and amenities

Thomson Reserve is surrounded by established low-rise private residential estates, including Soo Chow Gardens and Adelphi Park, as well as Windsor Park Estate , which is a Good Class Bungalow area.

Its elevated position offers panoramic views stretching from the surrounding landed estates to the city skyline, Singapore Island Country Club, Windsor Nature Park, the Central Catchment Nature Reserve and Bukit Timah Nature Reserve.

The Central Catchment Nature Reserve spans more than 3,000ha of forests and reservoirs, including MacRitchie Reservoir and Upper and Lower Peirce Reservoirs.

“What made this particular site especially compelling is also its scale and permanent natural setting,” says Liam. “The elevated topography, surrounding landed housing enclaves and proximity to the reservoirs and Central Catchment offer exceptional views and a sense of openness that is increasingly rare in Singapore.”

The development is a two-minute walk from Upper Thomson MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line, with sheltered access from the main entrance.

Ai Tong School is within walking distance, while Thomson Plaza is directly across Upper Thomson Road and accessible via an overhead bridge or the MRT station’s underground linkway.

Residents will also have access to the popular Upper Thomson dining stretch, which includes longstanding eateries such as Casuarina Curry, Nam Kee Chicken Rice and The Roti Prata House, alongside establishments such as Columbus Coffee Co, Filo Bistro, Salted Caramel and Omoté.

“Redeveloping [the Thomson View] site has given us an opportunity to build on the strengths of an established neighbourhood,” says CLD CEO (Singapore & International) Ronald Tay.

Two collections catering to different buyers

Thomson Reserve comprises two residential collections. The Classic Collection has 740 units across four 21-storey towers, while the Luxury Collection comprises 528 units in two 30-storey towers.

The Classic Collection offers two- to four-bedroom layouts, while the Luxury Collection features a mix of two-bedroom premium units to five-bedroom suites. Of the 528 units in the Luxury Collection, 112 larger four-bedroom premium units and five-bedroom suites feature private lift access.

Two-bedroom configurations make up  716 units (56.5%). Unit sizes range from 592 to 775 sq ft, with prices starting from $1.544 million ($2,608 psf).

Three-bedroom unit types account for another 350 units (27.6%), with sizes ranging from 947 to 1,152 sq ft. Prices start from $2.503 million ($2,643 psf).

Four-bedroom units account for 174 units (13.7%), ranging from 1,238 to 1,485 sq ft. Prices start from $3.388 million ($2,737 psf) for a 1,238 sq ft apartment.

At the top end are 28 five-bedroom suites, each measuring 1,808 sq ft. Occupying a single residential stack with unblocked views towards MacRitchie Reservoir and the Orchard Road skyline, they account for just 2.2% of the development.

The range of apartment sizes is intended to appeal to buyers at different stages of life. “While we expect interest from buyers familiar with the Upper Thomson neighbourhood, we believe its appeal extends beyond the immediate catchment to homebuyers across Singapore,” says CLD’s Tay.

He expects Thomson Reserve to attract first-time homeowners, young families and HDB upgraders, as well as existing private homeowners looking to upgrade or rightsize, and multigenerational families seeking larger living spaces.

Bringing the Central Catchment  into the development

The six residential towers occupy just 12% of Thomson Reserve’s site, leaving the remaining 88% for landscaping, water features and recreational facilities.

Designed by P&T Consultants, the towers have been oriented to maximise views of the surrounding greenery and minimise direct overlooking between blocks.

Inspired by the man-made contours of nearby MacRitchie Reservoir, P&T designed organically shaped pools and water features across the grounds to evoke a series of mini reservoirs.

More than 45% of the residential stacks face the Central Catchment Nature Reserve, while over 80% enjoy either greenery views or views of the development’s internal landscaping and waterscapes designed by Ecoplan Asia.

The development will have more than 80 facilities across three clubhouses, including eight swimming pools, two of which are 50m lap pools.

“Situated on one of the largest collective sale sites in recent history, the generous land size has allowed the developers to curate expansive greenery and comprehensive facilities,” says Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia, one of the three appointed joint marketing agents for Thomson Reserve, alongside PropNex and ERA.

Marcus Chu, CEO of ERA Singapore, believes the development’s elevated position and surrounding views will appeal particularly to buyers of higher-floor apartments. However, he considers the combination of greenery and convenience to be the stronger draw.

“Views may influence which unit a buyer chooses, but location and liveability are more likely to drive the decision to choose the development in the first place,” he says. Thomson Reserve is expected to obtain its temporary occupation permit in the second half of 2030.

Pent-up demand for new homes

The last mega condo launch in the immediate Upper Thomson–Shunfu area was JadeScape in 2018. Developed by Qingjian Realty, the project occupies the former Shunfu Ville site, a privatised HUDC estate that the developer acquired through an en bloc sale for $638 million in 2016.

JadeScape was subsequently fully sold and completed in 2022.

“Thomson Reserve represents the first new mega development of more than 1,000 units to be launched in the Bishan Planning Area in about eight years,” says Mohan Sandrasegeran, SRI’s head of research and data analytics.

It will be the UOL-CapitaLand joint venture’s second mega development in two years, following the 1,193-unit ParkTown Residence in Tampines. Launched in February 2025, ParkTown Residence sold 1,041 units, or 87%, during its launch weekend and is now 98% sold.

“We expect Thomson Reserve to garner healthy buyer interest owing partly to pent-up demand, its strong location attributes, and the wide selection of units at the development,” says Kelvin Fong, CEO of PropNex.

Mega developments tend to attract interest because of their wider range of unit types, greater market visibility and extensive recreational facilities, Fong adds.

For prospective buyers at Thomson Reserve, JadeScape also offers a useful pricing benchmark. Both are large 99-year leasehold developments in District 20, near MRT stations, and are redevelopments of private sites purchased en bloc.

According to ERA Research and Market Intelligence, JadeScape’s median resale price reached $2,341 psf in 2026, up 7.6% from 2023, based on caveats lodged as at Oct 13.

Meanwhile, SRI Research’s analysis of URA Realis caveats showed 253 resale transactions at JadeScape to date. All 253 transactions recorded gross gains for their respective sellers, based on the difference between their recorded purchase and resale prices, says Sandrasegeran.

Where will buyers come from?

PropNex’s sales data from JadeScape’s launch in 2018 and subsequent sales showed that about 53% of buyers served by the agency had HDB addresses. At the 372-unit Amo Residence , launched in 2022, the corresponding proportion was 46%. At both projects, just over a quarter of buyers served by PropNex lived in District 20.

“These figures suggest that new launches in the area can draw demand from a meaningful pool of HDB upgraders, as well as buyers already living in the district,” says PropNex’s Fong.

He expects HDB upgraders at Thomson Reserve to come from established estates such as Bishan and Ang Mo Kio, with interest likely to be concentrated in the larger two-bedroom and three-bedroom units.

Bishan recorded 79 HDB resale transactions of at least $1 million as at Oct 13, compared with 98 for the whole of 2025, according to ERA Research and Market Intelligence.

Another potential buyer group is landed homeowners looking to rightsize. ERA data shows that the median resale price of landed homes in District 20 has almost doubled from $1,152 psf in 2016 to $2,300 psf in the first nine months of 2026. This appreciation could allow owners to unlock some of their housing equity while remaining in a familiar neighbourhood, says ERA’s Chu.

He also sees potential demand for two-bedroom units from singles who want to live near their parents in the surrounding landed estates. “This allows families to stay connected while maintaining their own living space,” he says.

Larger three- to five-bedroom apartments, meanwhile, are expected to attract families seeking more space, while investors could be drawn by the development’s MRT connectivity and rental potential.

Huttons’ Yip estimates that existing private homeowners could account for about 80% of buyers at Thomson Reserve, with HDB upgraders making up the remaining 20%.

Rising land costs put future prices in focus

Beyond the resale market, the outcome of a recent Government Land Sale (GLS) tender in the neighbourhood provides another reference point for Thomson Reserve’s pricing.

The Lorong Puntong–Sin Ming Avenue residential site attracted seven bids when its tender closed on Sept 15. Malaysian developer Eco World Development submitted the highest offer of $208.1 million, or $1,612 psf ppr.

“The Lorong Puntong–Sin Ming Avenue GLS site tender is particularly interesting, as it gives us a glimpse of what developers are prepared to pay for future residential supply in this neighbourhood,” says ERA’s Chu. At $1,612 psf ppr, Eco World’s bid was approximately 37% higher than the $1,178 psf ppr land rate for the former Thomson View site. “This does not mean future selling prices will be 37% higher,” Chu says. “It suggests that the replacement cost of new homes in the Thomson-Bishan area is rising.”

With prices starting from $2,608 psf and a broad mix of two- to five-bedroom homes, Thomson Reserve will test buyers’ willingness to pay for a new home in one of Singapore’s established residential enclaves. Its appeal rests on a combination of connectivity, spacious homes, and views of the surrounding greenery.

"The private residential market has remained resilient, with buyers continuing to prioritise launches that offer strong transport connectivity, access to good schools and other amenities," says UOL Group's Liam. "Thomson Reserve brings these qualities together in one address, with interest expected from buyers drawn to the area’s established character and our strong product positioning."

article:
A decade ago, many investors questioned whether Singapore stocks could deliver capital growth, with the local market’s moribund state.
Yet, amid this scepticism,

Let’s check out what these sceptics missed about this once-unassuming financial technology player.
iFAST’s Humble Beginnings
iFAST was known for its Singapore-centric portal, distributing unit trusts through brands like Fundsupermart in 2000 and FSMOne in 2016.
Fast forward ten years to today (late 2026), iFAST is now a global digital banking and wealth management platform.
If you had held S$10,000 in iFAST shares back in 2016, your stake would be worth around S$100,000 today – roughly ten times the initial value.
Such returns aren’t just breathtaking, but potentially life-changing for some people.

Execution is key to iFAST’s dramatic rise.
The fintech player has come a long way since 2016, when it relied mostly on recurring fees from unit trusts on its platform.

Crucially, iFAST’s assets under administration (AUA) grew from S$6.10 billion in FY2016 to S$36.13 billion as of 30 June 2026.

Two operational catalysts.

iFAST continues to reward shareholders with dividend payouts.

Sunsine will need to find buyers for that extra output.

What matters is why the cash fell.
Cash tied up in inventories, receivables or supplier payments can flow back in later periods.
Sunsine’s shortfall came largely from working capital in a half when its gross profit grew 22%.
Delfi’s drop was also mostly working capital, though its thinner gross margin is a separate squeeze on earnings.
The next time a company raises its dividend in a weak cash half, ask yourself whether that cash will come back.

But that’s only part of the story.
Where is the growth coming from?
Demand for data centres is still the main engine.
The REIT manager points to forecasts that global data centre capacity will grow 25% a year to reach 256 GW by 2030.
What’s holding back the new supply isn’t money.
It’s power.
According to Keppel DC REIT, the hardest part of building a data centre is securing enough electricity and a grid connection, then winning planning approval.
These hurdles are steepest in established “Tier 1” markets such as Singapore, Japan and the major European hubs, where land and power are in short supply.
That scarcity plays to Keppel DC REIT’s strengths.
The REIT already owns operating data centres in exactly these markets, and clients have contracted around 95% of the power capacity it can earn revenue from.
How is Keppel DC REIT paying for its growth?
With more debt, though on better terms than a year ago:
Average cost of debt fell to 2.6% in 1H 2026 from 3.0% a year ago.
Interest cover rose to 6.9 times from 5.9 times.
Fixed-rate debt rose to 87% of borrowings from 76%.
A bigger debt load still costs more.

Gearing rose to 34% from 30%.
In short, Keppel DC REIT is carrying more debt at a lower
interest rate
.
That trade-off works as long as the newly acquired assets earn more than they cost, and net property income (NPI) growth of 15.1% to S$210.4 million suggests they do.
What are the risks?
Internet enterprise clients, mostly hyperscalers, accounted for 70.4% of rental income as of 30 June 2026, up from 67.4% a year earlier.
Here’s the rub: Keppel DC REIT’s single largest client contributes 43.5%.
This concentration cuts both ways.
Hyperscalers generally have higher credit quality and give investors direct exposure to AI-driven demand.
Unfortunately, Keppel DC REIT has not named its largest client.
Meanwhile, portfolio occupancy slipped to 92.5% in 1H 2026 from 95.8% a year ago.
Almost all of the decline comes from Cardiff Data Centre, whose contract expired in June 2026 and which now sits vacant.
Strip Cardiff out and portfolio occupancy would be 95.3%.
A few other assets still need work.
Keppel DC Singapore 1 remains at 46.5% occupancy after the non-renewal of its non-data-centre space, which makes up a significant portion of the asset.
The sale of Basis Bay, which has 40.2% occupancy, is taking longer than expected.
Keppel DC REIT announced the divestment on 2 January 2025 and had targeted completion by 3Q 2025.
In Guangdong, the manager has committed to no significant capital expenditure on its troubled data centres as it explores exit options.

A distribution, though, is only as dependable as the tenants who pay the rent.

title: Exporter dollar sales boost Malaysian ringgit, analysts say
article:
(Oct 15): Malaysian exporters are likely increasing conversions of their foreign-currency earnings into the ringgit, which stands to boost the local exchange rate through the rest of the year, analysts say.

Malaysia’s foreign-currency deposits fell 8.6% to RM308 billion ($97 billion) in August, the sharpest monthly decline since 2010, according to the most recent central bank data. The drop indicates that exporters, benefiting from semiconductor shipments, may be converting those earnings into ringgit.

While September trade figures are scheduled for release next week, BNP Paribas SA expects ongoing corporate conversions to support the ringgit. That momentum, combined with robust economic fundamentals and foreign direct investment inflows, should help lift the currency to 3.90 per dollar by June 2027 from around 4.08 currently, according to the bank.

“We expect corporate conversion flows to rise from onshore exporters seeking to reduce the rising FX exposure and from foreign direct investment inflows such as for the construction of data centres,” said Parisha Saimbi, EM Asia FX and rates strategist at the bank.

Malaysia approved RM225.97 billion of new data centre projects between February last year and July 2026 as the country continues to attract investment into cloud and AI infrastructure. The nation’s exports rose 45% in August from a year earlier, matching the growth seen in June, which was the fastest since August 2022.

See also: Taiwan dollar, won slump as chip selloff hurts Asian currencies

That has offered support for the ringgit, which rallied 1.5% against the dollar in August. Despite giving back some gains the following month amid a broader dollar rebound, it remains Southeast Asia’s best-performing currency this year behind the Singapore dollar.

Official efforts are reinforcing those market flows. Bank Negara Malaysia reiterated last month that it continues to encourage state-linked and private firms to repatriate and convert foreign-currency income. The strategy mirrors a similar move in South Korea, where officials urged exporters to repatriate overseas funds before the won began to recover.

With no official data on Malaysian exporter conversion of foreign currency proceeds into the ringgit, the size of business foreign-currency deposits held by commercial banks give an indication of such trends, according to Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at Australia & New Zealand Banking Group.

See also: Rupee’s relentless slide draws importers into RBI currency fight

“Since July there has been a fall in business foreign-currency deposits, which may point to increased conversion,” said Goh. “If there is a more noticeable rise in conversions, that should support the ringgit, though portfolio flows is also another important driver.”

title: TSMC’s profit surpasses expectations after AI orders rush in
article:
(Oct 15): Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) reported a better-than-expected profit for the September quarter, sustaining torrid growth despite rising concern about the long-term artificial intelligence (AI) buildout.

The global chipmaking linchpin said net income rose 69% to NT$763.1 billion (US$23.6 billion or $30.3 billion), more than the average analyst estimate. That came after the company reported a sales jump of 51% in the period, also above expectations, taking its revenue across the three months to US$47 billion ($60.3 billion).

The exclusive chipmaker of Nvidia Corp and Apple Inc’s most advanced semiconductors, TSMC offered a counterpoint to increasingly negative sentiment around AI-linked names. Downstream from the chipmaker, worries about return on investments and long-term financing are hurting companies like cloud provider and Nvidia customer CoreWeave Inc, which on Wednesday saw its stock and bond prices plunge in a widespread sell-off.

TSMC, for its part, has seen sales growth accelerate over the past two quarters and has ramped up capacity expansion. The company has said its capital expenditures will reach as much as US$64 billion, a record, this year.

Hsinchu-based TSMC serves as a key barometer of global AI demand as every major industry player including Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices Inc and Alphabet Inc’s Google rely on the Taiwanese chipmaker to turn their most cutting-edge designs into physical components.

See also: TSMC results face high bar to calm global AI stock trade jitters

TSMC’s shares touched a record this month, among the first chip stocks globally to set a new high after a July market rout. It’s been outperforming peers thanks to a dominant position in the manufacturing of processors needed to power AI. Yet it got caught up in the broader pullback in tech stocks over the past week.

Consensus estimates have been climbing for the Taiwanese firm’s 2027 capital spending, a key indicator for the industry. Goldman Sachs Group Inc now targets US$85 billion and UBS Group AG US$90 billion, compared with the US$75 billion average of firms polled by Bloomberg.

See also: Apple unveils US$299 HomeView Hub as part of new smart home push

The company is now trying to build and furnish about 20 factories at home and overseas, an unprecedented pace for a company that typically works on four or five new buildings simultaneously.

On top of its US$265 billion pledge to build a campus in Arizona, the company is now considering an additional US site in Texas due to the rush in the US to build data centres, Bloomberg News has reported.

title: Taiwan dollar, won slump as chip selloff hurts Asian currencies
article:
(Oct 15): The Taiwan dollar and South Korean won fell the most among Asian currencies as an overnight slump in Wall Street semiconductor shares spilled into regional markets, dampening demand for artificial intelligence supply-chain plays.

Taiwan’s currency fell as much as 0.8% while the island’s shares lost more than 3% in their sharpest drop since July. South Korea’s won declined as much as 1% with local shares down more than 8% and set for the lowest close since April. The risk-off sentiment spilled into Southeast Asia, putting pressure on currencies including the Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah.

Despite a broader currency selloff, the steep losses in North Asia underscore how deeply those export-reliant economies remain tethered to global technology sentiment. A US gauge of semiconductor stocks erased US$1.6 trillion in market value during a six-day losing streak on concerns over high interest rates, lofty valuations, and massive AI spending. The tech-led anxiety also spread across the region, knocking MSCI Inc’s Asia Pacific equities gauge down about 3%.

“The Korean won and Taiwan dollar, both proxies for the global tech cycle, have come under pressure amid the sharp selloff in technology stocks,” said Christopher Wong, a strategist at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp.

“Hotter US inflation overnight added to risk aversion, though the pullback in Treasury yields and oil prices may provide some offset,” he added.

See also: Exporter dollar sales bolster Malaysian ringgit, analysts say

The Taiwan dollar’s early-morning slump was primarily driven by foreign capital outflows and exporter dollar hoarding, according to traders. State-owned banks stepped in to sell greenbacks to provide market liquidity, said the traders who asked not to be named as they are not allowed to speak publicly.

Foreign investors dumped NT$165.3 billion of Taiwanese local equities on Tuesday, the third-biggest ever one-day outflow in data going back to 2000. Foreign outflows had extended to a sixth straight session on Wednesday.

In South Korea, foreign funds have dumped US$1.8 billion worth of Kospi equities on Thursday morning alone, pushing total monthly outflows past US$10 billion in October.

See also: Rupee’s relentless slide draws importers into RBI currency fight

“The stocks selloff is fuelling the global risk aversion, which is spreading to some Asian currencies,” said Philip McNicholas, Asia sovereign strategist at Robeco in Singapore.

“Those which are particularly vulnerable — currencies exposed to tech, obviously, as well as those which are exposed to risk sentiment like the rupiah and peso — are impacted the most,” he said.

Weak market sentiment reverberated well beyond North Asia on Thursday. The Philippine peso weakened past 63 per dollar for the first time. The Indonesian rupiah pared losses after the nation’s central bank intervened to steady the currency. The Reserve Bank of India sold dollars to support the rupee.

title: Singapore home sales recover from lowest level since 2024
article:
(Oct 15): Singapore new home sales rose in September from a more than two-year low, as developers resumed releasing projects after a brief pause.

Developers sold 296 new private units last month, according to figures released Thursday by the Urban Redevelopment Authority. That’s up from 153 homes sold in August, the fewest since February 2024, and 255 a year earlier.

The modest bounce reflects a return of new projects after the Hungry Ghost festival period, which ran from mid-August through Sept 10 and is widely seen as an inauspicious time for property purchases. At a time when interest rates are ticking up, the coming months will provide a clearer indication of whether a years-long boom that has defied multiple government curbs will regain steam.

Sales remained relatively subdued in September. Amberwood at Holland, a project partially released in the month, moved just over 10% of its 212 units in a popular expat enclave.

October is already shaping up to be a stronger month, with another 570-unit project in the country’s western suburbs selling about 60% of its units. New sales in the month are on track to exceed September’s.

See also: Malaysia's IOI Properties Group eyes US$760 mil property deals in Singapore

Demand from a mix of locals and wealthy immigrants has kept Singapore property values elevated. Prices of private homes rose 1.4% in the third quarter, up from 0.5% in the second, according to preliminary estimates released by the URA earlier this month. That was the fastest pace since 2024.

Chew, who is chairman of the National Parks Board, will join CDG’s board risk committee and sustainability committee. He will also assume chairmanship of the board risk committee from Jan 1, 2027.

He also previously served as chairman of the Workforce Singapore Agency from 2022 to 2026 and SimplyGo from 2024 to 2026.

Ang, who will join the group's audit committee and board risk committee, brings over 30 years of experience in audit, financial management, risk and capital-market transactions. title: IMF sees Asia’s growth slowing despite AI-fuelled resilience
article:
(Oct 15): The International Monetary Fund expects economic growth in the Asia-Pacific to slow this year and next, warning that rising energy prices and any pullback in the artificial-intelligence boom could test the region’s resilience.

Growth in the Asia-Pacific is projected at 4.8% in 2026, down from 5% last year but above the IMF’s April forecast of 4.4%. This will further moderate to 4.4% in 2027, the Washington-based fund said in its October regional economic outlook report.

The IMF raised its growth forecasts for most advanced economies, with projections revised up “sizably” for the likes of South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong that are reaping the benefits of the AI-driven investments surge. It also upgraded its outlook for China and India, while lowering predictions for countries facing higher inflation without comparable gains from technology demand.

The revisions highlight how strong demand for semiconductors, data centers and related technology products has helped cushion parts of Asia against mounting economic pressures. But the gains have been uneven, concentrated in economies plugged into global technology supply chains, the IMF said.

“Think of countries like Bangladesh, Cambodia, Laos, all these countries are importing oil. They are not benefiting from the AI boom that much. So these countries are a lot more vulnerable and they also have fewer policy buffers,” said Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF’s Asia and Pacific Department, in an interview with Bloomberg, adding that economies exposed to energy shocks but less integrated into global supply chains face greater risks.

See also: ECB may not have to do as much if markets tighten, Dolenc says

Some countries in Asia are already beginning to factor in a moderation in the AI tech cycle. Singapore’s central bank is expecting the boom to ease in latter half of 2027, following broader concerns from global policymakers about the sustainability of the trillion-dollar investment bonanza that’s betting on AI evolving at breakneck speed.

“Risks remain tilted to the downside,” the IMF said in its report. “A correction in AI-related investment or asset valuations could weigh disproportionately on Asia given its central role in global technology supply chains.”

Growth in emerging Asian markets and developing economies is expected to slow to 5.1% this year from 5.6% in 2025, before easing further to 4.9% in 2027, the fund said. Advanced economies in the region, meanwhile, are projected to expand 3.2% in 2026, up from 2.5% last year, before moderating to 2% in 2027.

See also: Germany to push EU to impose caps on more Chinese imports

The technology boom has also fuelled a rally in Asian equities, with valuations of regional technology stocks rising faster than their US counterparts this year. The IMF warned that elevated valuations, growing investor leverage and market concentration could increase the risk of significant turbulence.

Other risks cited by the report include a prolonged conflict in the Middle East that could keep energy prices elevated, rising global sovereign bond yields and a severe El Niño episode that could disrupt agriculture, fisheries and hydropower generation, adding to food and energy inflation.
