title: TSMC results face high bar to calm global AI stock trade jitters
article:
(Oct 15): With strong earnings from global chip majors failing to boost the AI trade, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co faces a high bar to impress investors.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has shed more than US$1.5 trillion in market value over the past six sessions on concerns over interest rates, financing for the AI buildout and the longevity of the chip cycle. TSMC shares fell as much as 2.8% in early Thursday trading in Taipei, ahead of its detailed earnings report due after the close.

TSMC, the world’s largest foundry, has already reported a 51% surge in quarterly sales. Still, solid recent results from Samsung Electronics Co and ASML Holding NV have done little calm market anxiety over chip shares.

“The bar is very high,” said Kevin Net, a portfolio manager at Financiere de L Echiquier. “To get a positive share price reaction, I think we need more than just a beat.” He’s looking for high margins and capital spending from TSMC, as well as signals of strong demand for AI and high-performance computing.

TSMC touched a record high earlier this month, among the first chip stocks globally to refresh its high after the July rout. It has been outperforming peers in the past few months thanks to its dominant position in outsourced manufacturing of processors needed to power the continued flood of new AI agents from major tech firms like Meta Platforms Inc.

See also: Apple unveils US$299 HomeView Hub as part of new smart home push

Yet it got caught up in the broader pullback in chip shares over the past week amid concerns over AI funding. Against this backdrop, TSMC’s results and guidance will be scrutinised to validate the sector’s growth narrative.

“The key readacross is whether TSMC turns more bullish on the duration and scale of AI demand,” said James Ooi, market strategist at Tiger Brokers. A bump in management’s AI accelerator revenue forecast or detail on the size of the gap in supply and demand for advanced chipmaking would be welcomed, he said.

See also: ASML’s guidance key to instill confidence in fragile chip trade

Consensus estimates have been climbing for the Taiwanese foundry’s 2027 capital spending, which is seen as a key metric for its share price. Goldman Sachs Group Inc now targets US$85 billion and UBS Group AG sees US$90 billion, compared with the US$75 billion average of firms polled by Bloomberg.

“Capex remains the utmost focus, as the company will likely continue to publicly state it remains committed to fulfilling backlogged customer demand,” JPMorgan Chase & Co’s sales desk wrote in a note to clients this week.

Another critical test is how well TSMC can protect its margins as it ramps up spending. Analysts estimate its gross margin at 66.5% for the three months through September, near the top of the company’s guidance range even if down slightly from the record level posted for the previous quarter.

“We are seeing a very long lasting cycle compared to historical standard, which is positive,” said Christophe Leroy, co-CIO and head of investment services at CBH Bank. “But at some point, we will see a cyclicality in the margin and you have to take into consideration what justify the current valuation.”

Investors will also closely parse TSMC’s commentary for indications of the impact from power grid constraints, regulatory hurdles or localised resistance to data centre construction.

“The market needs the whole AI ecosystem to work so if TSMC can demonstrate not only the demand is strong, but also the execution is also as planned,” said Xiadong Bao, a fund manager at Edmond de Rothschild Asset Management. For the AI capex narrative to continue, TSMC should continue to deliver on agentic AI promise, get strong commitments from hyperscalers and better manage bottlenecks, he added.

title: ECB may not have to do as much if markets tighten, Dolenc says
article:
(Oct 15): A tightening in financial conditions may limit the need for European Central Bank monetary policy action, according to Governing Council member Primoz Dolenc.

“We’ve seen quite a bit of repricing in the markets,” Dolenc told Bloomberg Television in Bangkok, where he’s attending the International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings. “If there is a tightening on the financial market, then maybe we don’t have to do as much as we would otherwise.”

After two hikes, policymakers are debating how much further interest rates will have to rise to return an inflation rate approaching 4% back to their target. Price pressures turned out stronger than expected in September, while the economy has proven more resilient than thought.

Economists are anticipating a final move in December, which would take the deposit rate to 2.75% — a level estimated by some to start restraining economic activity.

Asked about that prospect, Dolenc said that the ECB is “approaching the restrictive area — probably we are still not there, but we are on the limits.”

Governing Council members Pierre Wunsch and Gediminas Simkus — from Belgium and Lithuania, respectively — both highlighted the latest inflation data when arguing in separate Bloomberg interviews that more tightening will probably be needed. While a move in December would be based on more data, action this month can’t be excluded, the latter said.

See also: Germany to push EU to impose caps on more Chinese imports

“We have the situation that second-round effects are not visible or not visible yet,” Dolenc said, echoing similar comments from Simkus and ECB president Christine Lagarde earlier this week.

Any decision will be complicated by investor concerns about the fiscal situation in France and other highly indebted members of the 21-nation euro zone. The country led a recent bond-market selloff that propelled the 10-year yield to highs not seen in almost a quarter century.

Bank of France governor Emmanuel Moulin argued that higher sovereign borrowing costs are putting pressure on financial conditions, potentially damping demand — as well as inflation.

See also: Canada aims for India trade deal by year-end, minister says

Meantime, economists and investors are speculating how much worse the market situation needs to get before the ECB would be willing to step in.

“We have different monetary policy measures in our toolkit, even TPI,” Dolenc said. “They will be used or they would be used if necessary if the conditions are met. It’s really difficult to speculate right now when, how, and why different kind of tools will be used.”

Lagarde, a Frenchwoman herself, put the ball in the court of President Emmanuel Macron’s government, encouraging politicians to work on reducing a deficit that’s spiralled to nearly twice the ceiling allowed by European rules. But she also told a group of finance ministers recently that the ECB has the instruments to deal with the situation if needed.

Rising government borrowing costs across developed economies in Europe, America and elsewhere are a major theme at the Bangkok gathering of global finance officials. IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva called on policymakers last week to take urgent action to reduce high debts and budget deficits.

title: Stock sell-off extends to Asia as chip rout deepens
article:
(Oct 15): A sell-off in global equities spread to Asia on Thursday morning as losses in chip stocks deepened after faster-than-expected US inflation fuelled bets that the Federal Reserve (Fed) will need to raise interest rates further. Treasuries rallied on haven demand.

MSCI Inc’s Asia-Pacific equities gauge slid 2.2%, heading for its lowest level since July. South Korea’s Kospi Index — a bellwether for artificial intelligence (AI) investments — led regional losses with a 7% drop as chipmakers Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc both sank more than 8%.

Tech sentiment remained weak, with Nasdaq 100 Index futures falling 0.8%. Asian losses followed a slide on Wall Street that pushed the Russell 2000 Index into a correction, while a closely watched gauge of US semiconductor stocks had its longest daily losing streak since May 2025.

The fastest US inflation in five months prompted traders to ramp up bets on further Fed tightening, raising the prospect of additional rate hikes, even if policymakers pause in October. While Treasuries initially sank after the data was announced, they recovered most of the losses on appetite for bond yields near multi-year highs. The dollar weakened.

Stubborn US inflation, fuelled by elevated oil prices since the Middle East war broke out, is raising the prospect of more aggressive Fed tightening. At the same time, equity markets are coming under pressure after a blistering rally in AI-related stocks, bringing the US market’s longest stretch of tranquility since before the Covid-19 pandemic to an end.

See also: Asian stocks rise on signal Fed may not need aggressive rate hikes

“Inflation fear has been the main character recently,” said Anna Wu, an investment strategist and founder of Floodlines Research. “With inflation moving the rate path upward, it hurts everything else.”

Treasuries extended their gains at the start of Asian trading as the sell-off in equities spurred demand for haven assets. Yields on benchmark 10-year notes fell six basis points to 5.12%, while those on policy-sensitive two-year securities slid seven basis points to 4.73%.

Gold recovered after three days of declines to trade at about US$4,140 ($5,307) an ounce. While global crude oil benchmark Brent fell 1.1% to US$104.94 a barrel, elevated fuel prices were a factor in pushing up the US September consumer price index.

See also: ICE plans futures for livestock in a bid to challenge CME Group

Fed chairman Kevin Warsh has vowed not to steer markets with his own near-term outlook for monetary policy. But the inflation surprise will heighten scrutiny of his remarks late Thursday New York time in Bangkok, where he is scheduled to appear in a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva.

Markets now price about 40 basis points of Fed hikes by the end of January, with the odds of an October move also edging up.

“It’s clear as ever that inflation is stubborn and moving in the wrong direction,” said Skyler Weinand at Regan Capital. “While we expect the Fed to pause on any rate changes in October, we expect rate hikes to resume in December.”

Market attention remains firmly on tech after CoreWeave Inc shares plunged as much as 17% on Wednesday. Its debt due in 2032, which investors bought at par four months ago, traded at less than 78 cents on the dollar.

Also, Anthropic PBC told prospective investors its third-quarter revenue hit US$16.8 billion, according to people familiar with the matter, as the AI model maker pushes ahead with plans to go public.

“The US CPI (consumer price index) surprise and CoreWeave bond sell-off are prompting investors to reassess financing risks across the AI sector,” said Jung In Yun, the chief executive officer of Fibonacci Asset Management Global.

title: Malaysia's IOI Properties Group eyes US$760 mil property deals in Singapore
article:
(Oct 15): Malaysian property tycoon Lee Yeow Seng is making waves as one of the most aggressive buyers of commercial real estate in Singapore, and he’s not done yet.

His IOI Properties Group Bhd is in exclusive talks and due diligence to purchase two property assets — Chijmes, a retail venue inside a former Catholic convent in its civic district, and the nearby Capitol Kempinski hotel, chief executive officer Lee said in an interview. He declined to disclose how much a final agreement will value the two assets at, citing ongoing negotiations.

Singapore developer Perennial Holdings has been trying to sell the Kempinski hotel, which was being marketed for about $600 million (US$468 million), according to people familiar with the matter. Chijmes was valued at $379 million at the end of 2025.

IOI’s debt-fueled buying spree has spurred a record year for real estate deals in Singapore. The firm is now courting investors for a new fund to ease the burden and give room for further expansion, as Lee seeks to challenge the wealthy clans that dominate the country’s property market.

“I’m a latecomer and I want to catch up with the rest,” the 47-year-old CEO said on the sidelines of a Forbes event in Singapore last week. “Most of them don’t share the vision of me.”

See also: Hongkong Land to seek stake in tycoon Ong Beng Seng’s Singapore assets — Bloomberg

Perennial controls about a third of Chijmes, and about 80% of Capitol Singapore, a broader complex that contains the hotel, as well as a retail mall and residential units. A vehicle backed by an unnamed Southeast Asian sovereign wealth fund has a minority stake in both assets, corporate records show. Other Chijmes investors include local food chain Breadtalk Group Pte Ltd and Ronald Ooi, the former chair and CEO of Kim Eng, a stock brokerage.

Representatives of Perennial, which is backed by investors including palm oil tycoon Kuok Khoon Hong and Chinese private equity veteran Fang Fenglei, didn’t respond to requests for comments.

IOI is in talks to bring high-end fashion brands into Chijmes to raise rents, which have been depressed by a predominance of food and beverage outlets, said Lee. It also wants a global ultra-luxury hotel brand to replace the Kempinski, he said.

See also: Singapore property investment sales hit $42.2 bil in 9M2026, surpassing 2025: Knight Frank

Lee’s Malaysia-listed firm, which has a large presence in its home country including one of the world’s largest malls, has splashed out on a range of Singapore properties in recent years. It gained full control of South Beach, an office complex that also houses his luxury penthouse and the JW Marriott hotel, after buying the majority stake from partner City Developments Ltd, which was looking to reduce debt. More recently, it bought office building Asia Square Tower 2, ballooning his commercial portfolio to $10 billion.

It’s also looking to form a joint venture with CapitaLand Investment Ltd, a property manager backed by Temasek Holdings Pte Ltd, to buy One Raffles Place, people familiar with the matter said in August. The iconic office complex is majority-owned by OUE REIT, which confirmed last week that it’s in exclusive discussions with the firms on a potential sale.

IOI’s rapid acquisitions have fuelled a surge in its borrowings, with its net debt rising to 85% of equity as of end-June. In 2024, its board rebuffed a proposal by Lee to acquire Shenton House in Singapore, amid concerns about heavy capital commitments in Singapore and Malaysia. Lee, who is a scion of a wealthy palm oil family in Malaysia, made the purchase on his own.

The firm eventually agreed to acquire the office building and its liabilities this month to redevelop it. Even with a planned Malaysia real estate investment trust listing, that’s expected to raise the firm’s gearing further. Lee said he aims to reduce the net debt to 30%-50% of its equity in the next three to five years.

His plans largely hinge on the success of a private fund, which Lee said will be set up in two months. He’s tapped ex-Pimco Prime Real Estate executive Varun Singh to oversee the vehicle, which will initially include two assets totalling $6 billion: the office portion of South Beach and the firm’s marquee office building IOI Central Boulevard Towers, whose tenants include Morgan Stanley and Jane Street Capital LLC.

Lee said the fund has courted investors including private equity firms, sovereign wealth funds and insurers, but declined to share names. It’s targeting an internal rate of return of 10%-11%, with semiannual distributions, he said.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The firm is looking to pare down its stake in the assets to about half, by marketing minimum holdings of about $500 million with a five to seven-year lockup. It will look to inject more of its Singapore assets into the fund during that period, and eventually list it as a REIT.

Lee is more optimistic about real estate prospects in Singapore than rival financial hub Hong Kong, saying the former doesn’t have the baggage of being fully absorbed back into China in 2047 and will continue to be favored by the wealthy and global companies.

Still, other bets in Singapore have stumbled, including IOI’s plans to build a city center luxury residential project with 683 homes. The firm is liable to pay a higher tax, having sold only about 15 units there. Lee said he has secured a short-term reprieve from Singapore authorities to next April and will keep appealing against paying the charge.

The firm is pivoting toward renting out its units to expats, he said, blaming a 60% levy imposed on most foreigner purchases in 2023 for the poor sales.

But he remains undeterred in investing in Singapore, saying lenders and the company’s board remains supportive. “If I can expand, why should I hold myself back?” he said. “No one has asked me to slow down.”

title: Oil holds gain as Middle East and Russia strikes threaten supply
article:
(Oct 15): Oil held a gain on Thursday as a flare-up in attacks from Russia to the Middle East threatened supply that only recently recovered to near pre-war levels.

West Texas Intermediate (WTI) held near US$95 ($122) a barrel, after rising 1% on Wednesday. Brent settled around US$106. A cargo ship sank after being struck by “unknown projectiles” as it transited the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran-backed Houthis continued to launch missile and drone attacks across Saudi Arabia.

Meanwhile, Russia accused Ukraine of attacking two oil refineries on Wednesday, flouting an “energy ceasefire” promoted by US President Donald Trump. Kyiv denied the claim, which Bloomberg couldn’t independently verify.

Brent has surged more than 70% this year as the US-Iran war roils energy markets. The depletion of stocks during the fighting has left global observed inventories 509 million barrels below pre-conflict levels, and on-land stockpiles near their lowest in at least a decade, the International Energy Agency said Wednesday, warning that supplies of diesel and other fuels will remain under pressure next year.

“If new attacks on oil infrastructure in the Middle East further disrupt petroleum supply in an already very tight physical market, energy costs and inflation would move even higher,” said Bart Melek, the global head of commodity strategy at TD Securities.

Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Ukrainian drones targeted refineries in the Saratov and Ryazan regions, Interfax reported. Ryazan, near Moscow, has a processing capacity of about 400,000 barrels a day and is among the largest oil refineries in the nation.

See also: Oil rises as Middle East attacks increase uncertainty over flows

In the Middle East, a growing number of oil tankers are avoiding areas where they would normally collect crude, suggesting increased Iranian attacks on shipping are complicating export logistics. Vessels capable of carrying at least 37 million barrels have stopped or changed course while heading toward loading areas off the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Oman, though there’s no clear evidence yet that Gulf flows have declined.

Prospects for a diplomatic easing of tensions remain uncertain. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the Islamic Republic’s aims aren’t “endless war" or prolonged talks, but that it seeks to “wear down the enemy so that it is forced to accept our demands”.

Meanwhile, oil production in the UAE climbed to record levels last month, according to the IEA. The former Opec member has been one of the most successful regional producers in restoring flows through the Strait of Hormuz.

See also: Trump’s diesel deal irks allies and is unlikely to reduce prices

In the US, the industry-funded American Petroleum Institute reported nationwide crude inventories fell 11.1 million barrels last week, according to a document seen by Bloomberg. If confirmed by official data on Thursday, that would be the biggest drop since June 2025.

title: US stocks fall on inflation woes as chip rout deepens
article:
(Oct 15): Stocks fell the most since July as a sell-off in chipmakers on Wednesday extended a decline that was fuelled by wagers the US Federal Reserve (Fed) will keep lifting interest rates to fight inflation.

The broad upswing in consumer prices reinforced bets on rate hikes even if the Fed pauses in October. The S&P 500 snapped its longest streak without a 1% drop in over six years. The Russell 2000 entered a correction. A gauge of chip giants sank 4.3%. CoreWeave Inc’s bonds hit levels that usually signal distress. Its chief said the market is acting “irrationally”.

A closely watched measure of semiconductor powerhouses such as Nvidia Corp and Broadcom Inc extended a six-day drop to about 12% amid mounting concerns about higher rates, lofty valuations and the massive cost of building artificial-intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

“While increased competition within AI, rising financing requirements, and higher rates may periodically add to volatility, we view this latest bout as more of a recalibration of expectations than a fundamental break in the AI investment story,” said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Chief Investment Office.

The equity retreat kindled investor demand for bonds with yields near multi-year highs. The latest inflation data had earlier triggered a plunge in Treasuries, prompting traders to briefly price in two Fed hikes by the end of January. Those bets faded. The dollar hit the highest since May 2025.

See also: Stocks bounce from lows on Williams’ rate remarks

“It’s clear as ever that inflation is stubborn and moving in the wrong direction,” said Skyler Weinand at Regan Capital. “While we expect the Fed to pause on any rate changes in October, we expect rate hikes to resume in December.”

Fed chairman Kevin Warsh has vowed not to steer markets with his own near-term outlook for monetary policy. But the inflation surprise will heighten scrutiny of his remarks late Thursday New York time in Bangkok, where he is scheduled to appear in a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva.

Inflation pressures are broadening beyond energy, suggesting the last mile back to target could remain bumpy and keep rates elevated, according to Jeff Roach at LPL Financial. The latest report complicates the Fed’s decision this month as the road back to price stability is looking increasingly difficult to navigate, he added.

See also: S&P 500 holds firm as banks report earnings, chipmakers slump

The question is whether firmer core inflation is enough to alter the Fed’s path, according to Seema Shah at Principal Asset Management. Markets are clearly unsettled, but the latest report is not strong enough to revive the case for an October hike, she said.

While the latest consumer price index raises concerns around inflation risks, the Fed has already communicated a gradual hiking process, according to TD Securities’ strategists including Oscar Munoz and Gennadiy Goldberg.

“Today’s report makes the chance of an October hike higher, but we still believe the Fed will hold and opt for December as the market is already doing some of the work for them,” they said.
